title: Lanzhou Beef Noodle Soup
description: Clear, spiced beef bone broth over hand-pulled-style wheat noodles with radish, herbs and a spoon of chili oil on the side — northern China's most famous breakfast noodle.

ingredients.note: hand-pulled if available, or store-bought fresh wheat noodles

steps: Blanch the beef shank and bones in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse off the scum.
Return the meat and bones to a clean pot, cover with fresh water, add the star anise, cinnamon, peppercorns and bay leaves, and simmer gently, partially covered, for 2 hours.
Lift out the beef shank once fork-tender, set aside to cool, then slice thinly; keep simmering the bones for another hour.
Add the sliced radish to the pot and simmer 20 minutes more until tender, then season the broth with soy sauce and salt and strain out the solids.
Make the chili oil: heat the oil until shimmering, pour it over the chili flakes in a heatproof bowl, and stir until fragrant.
Boil the noodles in a separate pot of water until just cooked, about 2-3 minutes, then drain and divide among bowls.
Ladle the hot broth over the noodles, top with sliced beef and radish, and finish with scallions, cilantro and a spoon of chili oil on the side.
tips: Skim the broth as it simmers rather than boiling hard, or it turns cloudy instead of clear.
The broth and beef can be made a day ahead and reheated; the noodles should always be cooked fresh to order.
kidNote: Serve the kids' bowls before adding chili oil at the table, and let them add it themselves so nobody gets more heat than they asked for.
nutritionNote: Rich in protein and gelatin from the beef and bones but the seasoned broth is high in sodium; salt to taste rather than following the full amount, and pile on the radish and herbs for freshness.

title: Zhajiangmian
description: Beijing's everyday noodle dish: thick wheat noodles tossed with a savoury-sweet ground pork and fermented bean paste sauce, topped with crisp raw cucumber matchsticks.

ingredients.note: or hoisin sauce mixed with a little dark soy

steps: Mix the sweet bean paste and yellow bean paste with the water until smooth and pourable.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium heat and cook the ginger until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the ground pork and break it up, browning it for 3-4 minutes until no longer pink.
Splash in the Shaoxing wine, then pour in the diluted bean paste and simmer, stirring often, for 10 minutes until glossy and thickened.
Stir in the diced onion and cook 3-5 minutes more until softened.
Boil the noodles until just cooked, 2-3 minutes for fresh noodles, then drain and divide among bowls.
Top each bowl with the pork sauce and a handful of cucumber matchsticks, then toss together at the table before eating.
tips: Keep the sauce on the thick side — it should coat the noodles, not pool at the bottom of the bowl.
kidNote: No adjustment needed; the sauce is savoury-sweet, not spicy, and kids usually like mixing it themselves.
nutritionNote: The fermented bean paste and pork are salty and fatty; go light on any extra soy sauce at the table and let the raw cucumber do the balancing.

title: Biang Biang Noodles
description: Shaanxi's wide, hand-slapped wheat noodles, chewy and belt-like, doused in sizzling chili oil, garlic, vinegar and soy — the dish the noise of the name imitates.
steps: Mix the flour, salt and water into a shaggy dough, knead 5 minutes until smooth, then rub the surface with oil and rest, covered, for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 6-8 pieces, roll each into a flat strip, coat with oil, and rest a further 20 minutes.
Take each strip and stretch it by slapping it against the counter, pulling from both ends, tearing a channel down the middle so it opens into one long wide noodle.
Boil the noodles in batches for 2-3 minutes until they float and are cooked through, then drain into serving bowls.
Pile the chili flakes, cumin, ground peppercorn and garlic on top of each portion of noodles.
Heat the oil until just smoking and pour it over the spice pile — it should sizzle loudly and bloom the aromas.
Add the soy sauces and vinegar, then toss everything together with the blanched bok choy and scallions before serving.
tips: If the dough tears instead of stretching, it hasn't rested long enough — let it rest another 15-20 minutes and try again; rushing this step is the most common failure.
Keep the dough well-oiled while resting so the strips don't dry out or stick together.
kidNote: Make the kids' portions before adding the chili and Sichuan peppercorn topping — toss their noodles with just soy sauce, vinegar and a little of the hot oil for flavour without the numbing heat.
nutritionNote: The tempered chili oil is generous with fat and the sauce is salty; spoon it on rather than drenching, and the blanched bok choy adds fibre to balance the bowl.

title: Wonton Noodle Soup
description: Hong Kong-style thin egg noodles in a clear, savoury broth with plump pork-and-shrimp wontons — light, bouncy and the classic late-night snack of Cantonese noodle shops.
steps: Combine the pork, shrimp, sesame oil, soy sauce, white pepper and cornstarch in a bowl and mix briskly in one direction until slightly sticky, about 2 minutes.
Place a small spoonful of filling in the centre of each wrapper, wet the edges, fold into a triangle and press the corners together to seal.
Bring the chicken broth to a simmer and season with salt; keep it hot but not boiling.
Bring a separate pot of water to a boil and cook the noodles until just tender, 1-2 minutes, then drain and divide among bowls.
In the same pot, boil the wontons for 4-5 minutes until they float and the filling is cooked through.
Ladle the hot broth over the noodles, top with the wontons, and garnish with scallions and a drizzle of sesame oil.
tips: A food processor pulses the pork-shrimp filling to a bouncy paste in under a minute if you don't want to mix by hand.
kidNote: No spice to adjust; cut the wontons in half for younger kids so they're easier to eat with a spoon.
nutritionNote: Most of the sodium here comes from the broth and the soy-seasoned filling, so taste before adding extra salt, and boiling rather than frying keeps the dish light on fat.

title: Scallion Pancakes
description: Flaky, oniony flatbread layered by rolling and coiling oiled dough into a spiral, then pan-frying until crisp outside and chewy within — a street-cart breakfast staple.

ingredients.note: or make traditional hot-water dough from 1.5 cups flour and 0.5 cup hot water

steps: Wash and dry the scallions thoroughly, then chop finely.
Stack 4-5 dumpling wrappers, brushing a little oil, a pinch of salt and a scattering of scallions between each layer.
Roll the stack out gently with a rolling pin into a thin, round pancake about 6 inches across; repeat to make 3 pancakes.
Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a flat-bottomed pan over medium heat and fry a pancake for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Repeat with the remaining pancakes, adding oil as needed.
Stir together the soy sauce, vinegar and garlic for the dipping sauce, and cut each pancake into wedges to serve.
tips: Dry the scallions completely before layering — wet scallions steam the dough instead of letting it crisp.
kidNote: No spice; kids usually prefer these plain with just a dip of soy sauce rather than the vinegar-garlic mix.
nutritionNote: Pan-frying in oil makes this rich in fat; blot briefly on paper towels after cooking and serve it as a side rather than the whole meal.

title: Chinese Breakfast Crepe
description: A thin, egg-crisped flour crepe folded around sweet bean and chili sauces, cilantro, scallions and a crunchy cracker, cooked to order on a street griddle — China's grab-and-go breakfast.

ingredients.item: romaine lettuce leaves or wonton crackers

steps: Whisk the flour, salt and warm water into a smooth, pourable batter; let it rest 1 hour, covered, at room temperature.
Heat a lightly oiled non-stick skillet over medium heat and pour in a thin layer of batter, swirling to coat the pan.
Crack an egg over the crepe while the top is still wet and spread it evenly across the surface.
Once the egg sets, flip the crepe and cook the egg side briefly, about 10-15 seconds.
Flip back egg-side up, spread with sweet bean sauce and chili bean sauce, then sprinkle with sesame seeds, scallions and cilantro.
Lay the lettuce or a cracker across the middle, fold both sides in, then roll up tightly and slice in half to serve warm.
tips: The batter rest is mostly unattended time — start it first, then prep your toppings while it sits.
kidNote: Spread the kids' crepes with just sweet bean sauce, skipping the chili bean sauce entirely; they still get the crunch and egg they like.
nutritionNote: The sweet and chili bean sauces are salty and sugary in small doses; use a light hand when spreading and let the egg, lettuce and herbs carry most of each bite.

title: Pan-Fried Pork Buns
description: Shanghai's crackle-bottomed buns: yeasted dough wrapped around a juicy pork filling, fried crisp on the base then steamed to finish, bursting with savoury broth in every bite.

ingredients.note: made from simmered pork skin and bones, chilled until set

steps: Combine the flour, yeast, sugar and warm water into a smooth dough, knead 10 minutes, then let it proof just 30 minutes so it stays slightly chewy rather than fluffy.
Mix the ground pork with soy sauces, sesame oil, ginger and scallions, then fold in the chilled aspic cubes without breaking them up too much.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces, flatten each into a disc, add a spoonful of filling, and pleat closed at the top.
Arrange the buns pleat-side up in a well-oiled non-stick pan, leaving space between them.
Fry over medium heat, uncovered, for 3-4 minutes until the bottoms are golden.
Add water to come a third of the way up the buns, cover, and steam for 8-10 minutes until the dough is cooked through.
Uncover, sprinkle with sesame seeds and scallions, and cook a final 2-3 minutes uncovered until the water evaporates and the bottoms re-crisp.
tips: The aspic can be made a day ahead and needs to be fully chilled and firm before mixing in, or the filling turns runny.
Handle the buns gently once filled — a torn wrapper lets the broth leak out during cooking.
kidNote: Not spicy, but the filling is very hot straight off the pan — let buns cool for a couple of minutes and warn kids about the hot broth inside before they bite in.
nutritionNote: The pork filling and aspic are rich in fat and the soy seasoning is salty, and pan-frying adds more oil still, so serve with a plain vegetable soup rather than more fried sides.

title: Steamed BBQ Pork Buns
description: Pillowy white steamed buns split open to reveal a sweet-savoury diced char siu pork filling in a glossy oyster sauce gravy — the dim sum cart favourite.
steps: Dissolve the yeast in warm water, then mix with the flour, cornstarch, sugar and oil into a smooth dough; cover and let rise 2 hours until doubled.
Meanwhile, sauté the shallots in oil until fragrant, add the oyster sauce, soy sauces and stock, and simmer with the flour whisked in until thickened.
Stir the diced char siu into the sauce, coat well, then cool completely in the fridge.
Knead the baking powder into the risen dough, then rest a further 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 10 pieces, flatten into discs, spoon in the cooled filling, and pleat closed at the top.
Set each bun on a square of parchment and rest 15 minutes before steaming.
Steam over high heat in batches for 12 minutes until puffed and glossy white; let the buns rest 2 minutes before opening the lid.
tips: Cool the filling fully before wrapping — warm filling softens the dough and makes it hard to seal.
kidNote: Not spicy; the sweet-savoury filling is one of the easiest dim sum items for kids to like.
nutritionNote: The oyster and soy sauces make the filling fairly salty, and the dough itself has added sugar and oil; balance the meal with steamed greens rather than more fried dim sum.

title: Pork and Shrimp Siu Mai
description: Open-topped steamed dumplings packed with a bouncy pork and shrimp filling and shiitake mushroom, topped with a fleck of carrot — a dim sum table essential.

ingredients.item: dried shiitake mushrooms, rehydrated and diced

steps: Rehydrate the shiitake mushrooms in warm water for 20 minutes, then drain and dice finely.
In a stand mixer or by hand, beat the ground pork with cornstarch, Shaoxing wine, oyster sauce, sesame oil, white pepper and salt for about 4-5 minutes until it turns pale and sticky.
Fold in the diced shrimp and mushrooms until evenly distributed.
Place a spoonful of filling in the centre of each wrapper and gently squeeze the sides upward around the filling, leaving the top open.
Tap each dumpling on the counter to flatten the base and press a few flecks of minced carrot into the top.
Line a steamer basket with parchment or cabbage leaves, arrange the dumplings with space between them, and steam over simmering water for 9 minutes until the filling is firm and opaque.
Serve hot, straight from the steamer, with chili oil or soy-vinegar dip on the side.
tips: These freeze well uncooked — steam straight from frozen, adding 2-3 minutes to the steaming time.
kidNote: Not spicy on its own; keep any chili dipping sauce off to the side so kids can eat theirs plain.
nutritionNote: Pork, shrimp and oyster sauce add up to a fairly sodium-heavy snack; steaming at least keeps added fat low, so pair with plain rice or vegetables rather than more fried dim sum.

title: Shrimp Dumplings
description: Delicate, translucent wheat-starch dumplings pleated tight around a juicy whole-shrimp and bamboo shoot filling — the benchmark dish dim sum cooks are judged by.

ingredients.item: raw shrimp, peeled and roughly chopped

steps: Mix the shrimp with oyster sauce, sesame oil, white pepper, ginger, salt and sugar; fold in the bamboo shoots and chill while making the dough.
Whisk the wheat starch and cornstarch together, then pour in the boiling water all at once, stirring rapidly until it forms a shaggy, translucent mass.
Add the lard and knead the hot dough until smooth, keeping it covered with a damp towel between steps so it doesn't dry out.
Roll the dough into a log and divide into 18 equal pieces, flattening each into a thin round with the flat side of an oiled cleaver or a small rolling pin.
Place a spoonful of filling in the centre of each wrapper and pleat one edge around the other, sealing into a crescent shape.
Line a steamer with parchment, arrange the dumplings with space between them, and steam over high heat for 6 minutes until translucent.
Serve immediately — har gow does not reheat well, so time the steaming for right before eating.
tips: The water must be fully boiling when you pour it into the starch, or the dough won't turn translucent and will crack when rolled.
If the wrapper cracks while rolling, it's too dry — knead in a few drops of hot water and keep unused dough covered.
Expect the wrapping to take practice; even experienced dim sum cooks spend a long time getting the pleating even.
kidNote: Not spicy and easy for kids to eat; just watch that the shrimp filling is cooked through and fully opaque before serving.
nutritionNote: Steaming keeps this genuinely low in added fat, though the filling is seasoned with oyster sauce and sesame oil for sodium — one of the lighter dim sum choices in this batch.
